'''''Leonotis nepetifolia''''', (also known as '''klip dagga''', '''Christmas candlestick''', or '''lion's ear'''<ref name="Napier">{{cite web|last1=Napier|first1=E.|title=NOTES· ON WILD FLOWERS|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/content/part/EANHS/Nos.%2047-48_138_1933_Napier.pdf|publisher=biodiversitylibrary.org|access-date=31 December 2017}}</ref>), is a species of [[plant]] in the [[genus]] ''[[Leonotis]]'' and the family [[Lamiaceae]] ([[Mentha|mint]]), native to tropical Africa and the Indian Subcontinent.<ref name=CABI/><ref>{{cite web |last1=Hutchings |first1=Ed |title=Mr |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:127310-3 |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Yew}}</ref> It can also be found growing abundantly in much of [[Latin America]], Southeast Asia, the [[West Indies]],<ref name=CABI/> and the [[Southeastern United States]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Plants Profile for Leonotis nepetifolia (Christmas candlestick)|url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=LENE|access-date=2021-03-10|website=plants.usda.gov}}</ref> It grows to a height of {{convert|3|m|ftin}} and has whorls of striking lipped [[flower]]s, that are most commonly orange,<ref name="Napier"/> but can vary to red, white, and purple. It has drooping dark green, very soft serrated [[Leaf|leaves]] that can grow up to {{convert|4|in|cm|order=flip}} wide.<ref name="Napier"/> [[Sunbird]]s and [[ant]]s are attracted to the flowers.<ref name="Napier"/> It has been found growing on roadsides, rubbish heaps or waste land.<ref name="Napier"/>

''L. nepetifolia'' is considered an [[Invasive species|invasive plant]] in [[Australia]], [[Florida]], and [[Hawaii]], though its tendency to grow in disturbed areas led researchers in Hawaii to conclude it's not likely to be an ecological threat.<ref name=CABI>{{Cite web|date=26 April 2015|title=''Leonotis nepetifolia'' (Christmas candelstick)|url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/110266#:~:text=L.-,nepetifolia%20is%20a%20large%20upright%20herbaceous%20plant%20native%20to%20tropical,Florida%20(Floridata%2C%202014).|access-date=11 April 2025|website=CABI Invasive Species Compendium}}</ref>

== Related species ==
''Leonotis  nepetifolia'' (''klip dagga'') is related to ''[[Leonotis leonurus|L. leonurus]]'' (''wild dagga'' or ''lion's tail''.) The most noticeable difference between the two is the leaf shape. ''L. nepetifolia'' leaves are [[Leaf shape|cordate]] with serrated edges, except the top pair which are [[Leaf shape|lanceolate]] with serrated edges, as pictured in taxonomy box. The leaves are all lanceolate with serrated edges on ''L. leonurus''.

== Traditional medicine ==
''Leonotis nepetifolia'' is known in [[Trinidad]] as ''shandilay'' and the leaves are brewed as a tea for [[fever]], [[cough]]s, womb prolapse, [[malaria]], and suggested to be beneficial to bone and lung health. The roots of ''L. nepetifolia'' are considered to be the botanical sources of ''granthiparna'', an [[Ayurveda|ayurvedic]] herb.{{cn|date=March 2021}}

==Phytochemicals and pharmacology==
[[File:Lucifer Hummingbird, Laguna de Acuitlapilco imported from iNaturalist photo 6017775.jpg|thumb|[[Lucifer sheartail]] feeding on its nectar]]
Leonotis nepetifolia and [[Leonotis leonurus|wild dagga]] contains several labdane diterpenes including Hydroxynepetaefolin, Nepetaefuran, Nepetaefolinol, Nepetaefolin, Leonotinin, Leonotin and Dubiin as well as bispirolabdane diterpenes like Leonepetaefolin A-E.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Jun |last2=Fronczek |first2=Frank R. |last3=Ferreira |first3=Daneel |last4=Burandt |first4=Charles L. |last5=Setola |first5=Vincent |last6=Roth |first6=Bryan L. |last7=Zjawiony |first7=Jordan K. |title=Bis-spirolabdane Diterpenoids from Leonotis nepetaefolia |journal=Journal of Natural Products |date=27 April 2012 |volume=75 |issue=4 |pages=728–734 |doi=10.1021/np3000156 |pmid=22475308 |pmc=3338874 |bibcode=2012JNAtP..75..728L }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Blount |first1=John F. |last2=Manchand |first2=Percy S. |title=X-Ray structure determination of methoxynepetaefolin and nepetaefolinol, labdane diterpenoids from Leonotis nepetaefolia R.Br. |journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Perkin Transactions 1 |date=1 January 1980 |pages=264–268 |doi=10.1039/P19800000264 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Barbosa |first1=Jackson de Menezes |last2=Cavalcante |first2=Noelly Bastos |last3=Delange |first3=David Marrero |last4=Almeida |first4=Jackson Roberto Guedes da Silva |title=A review of the chemical composition and biological activity of Leonotis nepetifolia (Linn.) R. Br.(lion's ear) |journal=Revista Cubana de Plantas Medicinales |volume=23 |issue=4 |year=2018 |url=http://www.revplantasmedicinales.sld.cu/index.php/pla/article/view/687/346 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190606150535/http://www.revplantasmedicinales.sld.cu/index.php/pla/article/view/687/346 |archive-date=6 June 2019 }}</ref>

[[Docosatetraenoylethanolamide]] (DEA) has been identified in Leonotis nepetifolia flower petals.<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/346796873 |doi=10.1186/s13104-020-05372-z|title=Toward the identification of a phytocannabinoid-like compound in the flowers of a South African medicinal plant (Leonotis leonurus) |year=2020 |last1=Hunter |first1=E. |last2=Stander |first2=M. |last3=Kossmann |first3=J. |last4=Chakraborty |first4=S. |last5=Prince |first5=S. |last6=Peters |first6=S. |last7=Loedolff |first7=Bianke |journal=BMC Research Notes |volume=13 |issue=1 |page=522 |pmid=33172494 |pmc=7653773 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Methanol based extracts of Leonotis nepetifolia has shown antidepressant-like effects in mice. Metabolic screening of the extract suggested nepetaefolin, methoxynepetaefolin, and 7-O-β-glucoside luteolin are the main products.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Arrieta-Báez |first1=Daniel |last2=Gómez-Patiño |first2=Mayra Beatriz |last3=Jurado Hernández |first3=Noé |last4=Mayagoitia-Novales |first4=Lilian |last5=Dorantes-Barrón |first5=Ana María |last6=Estrada-Reyes |first6=Rosa |title=Antidepressant-like effects of a methanol extract of Leonotis nepetifolia in mice |journal=Natural Product Research |date=31 March 2022 |volume=36 |issue=23 |pages=6170–6176 |doi=10.1080/14786419.2022.2058939 |pmid=35357257 |s2cid=247842622 |url=https://figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/19487422 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Nepetaefuran and leonotinin isolated from Leonotis nepetaefolia plant material demonstrated anti-inflammatory by suppressing [[NF-κB]] activation related to proinflammatory [[Cytokine]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ueda |first1=Fumihito |last2=Iizuka |first2=Keito |last3=Tago |first3=Kenji |last4=Narukawa |first4=Yuji |last5=Kiuchi |first5=Fumiyuki |last6=Kasahara |first6=Tadashi |last7=Tamura |first7=Hiroomi |last8=Funakoshi-Tago |first8=Megumi |title=Nepetaefuran and leonotinin isolated from Leonotis nepetaefolia R. Br. potently inhibit the LPS signaling pathway by suppressing the transactivation of NF-κB |journal=International Immunopharmacology |date=1 October 2015 |volume=28 |issue=2 |pages=967–976 |doi=10.1016/j.intimp.2015.08.015 |pmid=26319953 }}</ref>
